claim: Among Chinese livestreamers, only 5% earned more than 10,000 yuan (about USD 1,500) per month while more than 70% earned less than 100 yuan (about USD 15) per month -- a roughly hundred-fold gap between the top ventile and the bottom seven deciles.
stance_target: The claim that creator income distributions are extremely unequal and that the modal creator earns far below any living-wage threshold
scope_conditions: China, circa 2017; attributed to a Tencent Research Institute report cited via a press account (Meng 2017b); underlying sample size, sampling frame and methodology NOT stated in the paper -- an industry estimate, not a verified measured distribution; NOT Southeast Asia
quoted_support: only 5 per cent made more than 10,000 yuan ($1500 USD) a month, while and more than 70 per cent said they earned less than 100 yuan ($15 USC) a month

claim: The modal Chinese livestreamer's reported monthly earnings of about USD 15 is roughly one-seventeenth of the developing-Asia living wage of USD 254 per month, so livestreaming is for most participants not a marginal income source but a negligible one.
stance_target: The claim that 'creator' should not be treated as an occupation for the majority of people doing it, because typical earnings are orders of magnitude below subsistence
scope_conditions: China, circa 2017; combines the Tencent Research Institute income figure cited here with the ADB Institute developing-Asia living wage; both are estimates from different years and the comparison is an inference, not a finding in either source
quoted_support: with a reported 3.5 million commercial livestreamers, 5 percent translates into hundreds of thousands successful livestreamers

claim: Published market-size estimates for the Chinese livestreaming industry diverge by more than a factor of two for adjacent years -- USD 5bn (2016), USD 4.4bn (2017), USD 10bn (2018) -- demonstrating that industry-sourced creator-economy figures are not reconcilable with each other.
stance_target: The reliability of vendor and consultancy market-size figures as a basis for inferring creator income
scope_conditions: China, 2016-2022 forecasts; figures compiled from Moshinsky (2016), Lavin (2018) and iResearch (2018); the authors present the divergence itself as their point
quoted_support: Estimates of the value of livestreaming range from $US5 billion in 2016 (Moshinsky, 2016) to $US4.4 billion in 2017 (Lavin, 2018) to $US10 billion in 2018 with predictions for $US19 billion in 2022 (iResearch, 2018).

claim: The paper's own creator evidence comes from 22 interviewees recruited by snowball through platform executives and university alumni networks, of whom fewer than half were livestreamers -- an access-gated sample that systematically over-represents survivors.
stance_target: The claim that survivorship bias is the dominant failure mode in creator-economy research, because samples are recruited through industry gatekeepers who know only successful creators
scope_conditions: China, fieldwork 2017, Beijing/Shanghai/Guangzhou; qualitative interview study
quoted_support: Among 22 interviewees, nearly half were with livestreamers working either full or part time ... Livestreamers were introduced by platform executives and our connections through alumni and events at USC Annenberg and Shanghai Jiao Tong University.

claim: More than 3 million YouTube creators globally received some level of remuneration, and in mid-2018 only about 5,000 YouTubers worldwide had at least one million subscribers -- so top-tier visibility is on the order of 0.2% of monetized creators.
stance_target: The claim that the visible tier of successful creators is a vanishingly small fraction of the monetized creator base, which is itself a fraction of all creators
scope_conditions: Global, mid-2018; figures cited by the authors without full attribution in the accepted manuscript; WESTERN/GLOBAL, not SEA-specific
quoted_support: more than 3 million YouTube creators globally receive some level of remuneration from their uploaded content and it is estimated that, in mid-2018, the top five thousand YouTubers globally had at least one million subscribers

claim: US creators earned USD 5.9bn across nine digital and social media platforms in 2016 according to the Re-Create Coalition (Shapiro and Aneja 2018), a figure that must be divided across millions of creators to yield a per-creator average.
stance_target: Establishing a US aggregate creator-earnings denominator for comparison with the ~USD 3bn Southeast Asian e-commerce influencer fee pool
scope_conditions: United States, 2016; secondary citation of an advocacy-coalition report (Re-Create Coalition), methodology not described in this paper; WESTERN-ONLY, does not generalise to Southeast Asia
quoted_support: A report by the Re-create Coalition stated that Creators earned $5.9b across 9 digital and social media platforms in 2016 in the United States alone (Shapiro and Aneja 2018).
